items.rationale: The model only classifies; the code decides what each label leads to, so the code still owns the control flow. Branching on a model's output is still a fixed workflow.

With one to six checks in 41 orders, and results redirecting the path, the next step must be chosen at run time by the model in a loop. A fixed order, a single call or a route fixed up front cannot adapt mid-way.

items.answer: Nothing: the path is the same every time, so the model choosing each step adds cost without benefit.

items.rationale: The traces were identical, so the model's per-step decisions changed nothing while adding four calls per form. A learner who answers 'flexibility' or 'accuracy' treats a loop as the default.

With unknown variation and a small budget, start with the simplest fixed design and add model-chosen steps only where measured failures show the need. A loop or several loops pays cost first; keeping the fixed sequence regardless ignores that it may fail.
The failure exists because the model owns the order; code that runs the check first guarantees it. Prompt rules, a larger model or a status tool only make the right order more likely, not certain.

Bookings follow the same calls every time and the request type is known, so code can run them cheaply and reliably; the loop stays where the path varies. A higher cap, examples or a second loop keep the model in charge of a path that needs no decision.
